title: Why do cats drink so little?
excerpt: Cats naturally have a low sense of thirst.
body: Cats naturally have a weak sense of thirst, inherited from their desert ancestors, who drew most of their water from the prey they ate.
Insufficient hydration raises the risk of urinary stones and kidney problems, which are especially common in older cats.
Favouring wet food, placing several water bowls around the home and using a water fountain can all encourage a cat to drink more.

title: Why hydration is essential
excerpt: Water supports a cat's kidneys and urinary tract.
body: Water plays a part in digestion, temperature regulation and the elimination of waste by the kidneys.
A cat fed exclusively on dry food rarely drinks enough to make up for the lack of moisture in its ration.
A clean bowl, kept away from the litter tray and from the food, is often better accepted by the cat.

title: How to choose the right dry food
excerpt: The ingredient list tells you almost everything about a kibble.
body: The ingredient list should always be read first: animal proteins must appear at the top of the list.
Avoid kibble containing large amounts of cereals or poorly identified animal by-products.
Match your choice of kibble to your cat's age, activity level and state of health.

title: Recognising the signs of stress in cats
excerpt: Stress shows up in behaviour above all.
body: A stressed cat may hide more, urinate outside the litter tray or groom itself excessively.
Changes in environment, the arrival of a new animal or noise are frequent triggers.
Providing safe retreats and respecting the cat's routine helps to lower its stress level.

title: Why the cat is an obligate carnivore
excerpt: Its needs can only be met by animal tissue.
body: Nutritionally, the cat is classified as an obligate carnivore: its metabolism creates requirements that can only be met by a diet containing animal tissue, in particular for taurine, arginine, arachidonic acid, vitamin A and vitamin D.
The cat has at least 45 essential nutrients, and its requirements for protein, taurine, vitamin A or niacin are higher than those of an omnivore.
It can digest some nutrients of plant origin, but a vegetarian diet cannot cover its needs.
Sources: Merck Veterinary Manual, Royal Canin Academy.

title: Taurine, a nutrient cats cannot make
excerpt: An essential amino acid that has to come from food.
body: Taurine is an essential amino acid for cats: it is involved in vision, heart muscle function, digestion, and the nervous, immune and reproductive systems.
Unlike most mammals, the cat synthesises very little of it and loses it continuously in the digestive tract through the conjugation of bile salts.
Meat, offal and fish are rich in it; cereals provide only marginal or insufficient amounts.
Since 1987, cat foods meeting AAFCO standards have been required to contain a minimum level.
Sources: dvm360, VCA Animal Hospitals, AAFCO.

title: Portions and excess weight: what really counts
excerpt: Portion control is the key to calorie intake.
body: Excess weight appears when a cat takes in more energy than it uses: portions that are too large, frequent treats, an indoor life, food left out free-choice.
In cats, obesity raises the risk of diabetes and hepatic lipidosis, and comes with a higher frequency of urinary and joint problems.
Portion control remains the main lever: weigh the ration, split it into measured meals, and count treats in the daily total.
Weight loss should be slow, around 0.5 to 2% of body weight per week, and monitored by a vet.
Sources: dvm360, VCA Animal Hospitals, Association for Pet Obesity Prevention.

title: Switching foods without digestive upset
excerpt: A gradual transition over 7 to 10 days.
body: An abrupt food change often causes vomiting, diarrhoea or refusal of the bowl: the gut flora and digestive enzymes need time to adapt.
The recommended transition spreads over 7 to 10 days, replacing about a quarter of the old food every two days.
Some cats that are sensitive, older, or have eaten the same food for years need 14 days or more.
A cat that stops eating for more than 24 hours should be seen promptly by a vet.
Sources: Purina Institute, PetMD, AAHA.

title: Feeding the senior cat
excerpt: After 11 years, energy requirements rise again.
body: Cats enter their mature phase around 7 years of age, and are considered senior from 10 to 11 years.
Their digestive capacity declines: roughly 30 to 40% of older cats digest fats and proteins less well. Energy requirements first fall, then rise again around 11 years.
Contrary to a widespread belief, a healthy older cat should not be restricted in protein: it protects its muscle mass.
Renal diets, restricted in protein and phosphorus, are reserved for cats diagnosed with chronic kidney disease.
Sources: AAHA/AAFP Feline Life Stage Guidelines, VCA Animal Hospitals.

title: The cat's hunting mode
body: A cat living solely on what it catches would need to take roughly 10 to 20 prey a day, while each hunting attempt has less than a 50% chance of succeeding.
That constraint is what explains the behaviour: cats evolved to attempt a hunt whenever the opportunity arises, hungry or not. The sight or sound of prey is enough to trigger the sequence.

A stray cat spends an average of 12 hours a day hunting, against about 3 hours for an owned cat. The number of prey follows the same gap: on the order of 27 a year for a well-fed cat, against more than 270 for a stray.
Hunting activity also varies with age, physical condition, temperament, neutering and food security. It is strongest from spring through autumn.
A full bowl does not remove the need: daily play sessions that reproduce the stalk, chase and capture sequence reduce aggression and dawn wake-ups.
Sources: International Cat Care via Purina, LPO, Vetopsy.

title: Overweight cats
excerpt: Neutering, indoor life and middle age compound each other.
body: Excess weight is now one of the most common nutritional disorders in cats. Estimates vary widely by country: about 11.5% in the United Kingdom, 15.7% in Australia and 41% in the United States, with some populations reaching 63%.
The identified risk factors converge: oversized portions, low energy expenditure, an unstimulating environment, an exclusively dry diet, a strictly indoor life, male sex and neutering.
Neutering is the best established factor: neutered cats are more than three times as likely to be overweight as entire cats, because of hormonal changes that reduce activity and increase food intake.
Prevalence rises from 2 to 3 years of age, peaks between 5 and 11 years, then tends to fall in older cats.
The consequences are documented: diabetes, insulin resistance, hepatic lipidosis, urinary problems, arthritis and lameness, skin disease, and a shorter life expectancy.
Owners often underestimate their cat's body condition: an assessment by a vet remains the reference point before starting any weight loss.
Sources: Veterinary Record 2025, Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery.

title: Litter box: plastic or stainless steel?
excerpt: Hygiene against comfort: both have a case.
body: Plastic is porous. Over time, acidic urine and claw marks create micro-scratches where bacteria settle, out of reach of cleaning products, which keeps a persistent smell alive despite washing.
That is why a plastic tray used by an adult cat should generally be replaced every 6 to 12 months to keep hygiene acceptable.

Stainless steel is non-porous: it holds neither fluids nor odours, cleans with a simple rinse, is dishwasher-safe, does not scratch under claws and lasts for years. It is also recyclable and gives off no chemical smell when new.

Stainless steel has real drawbacks that often go unmentioned: colder underfoot, and noisier when the cat digs or when the litter is sifted. Some sensitive cats hesitate to step in, or dig less willingly.
Non-slip pads under the tray and a thick enough layer of litter soften both the noise and the cold. When switching, leave the old tray in place for a few days and let the cat choose.
A cat with a history of urinary problems, or unexplained soiling, is the case where switching to stainless steel is most justified.
Sources: Gizmo, Les Trésors d'Owka, Avis Litière.
